cues.text: Imagine a small grey room.

A federal agent slides a recorder
across a steel table and presses play.
And the voice that comes out, calm,

certain, talking about a stock
days before the news breaks,
is yours. There is no arguing with it.
There is no explaining it away.

It is simply you, on tape,
in your own words.

This film is the story of the first time
the untouchables of Wall Street heard
that sound.

For a long time, almost everyone on Wall
Street believed the same quiet thing.
That at the very top, the game was rigged.

That a small handful of people always
seemed to know — about the merger,
the bad quarter, the secret deal — a day,
or an hour, before the rest of the world.

You could see it
in the timing of the trades.
You could feel it in your gut.
You just could never, ever prove it.

The man at the center of this story
ran a hedge fund called Galleon.

At its peak it managed
about seven billion dollars.
He was a billionaire.

He was charming, brilliant,
generous to his friends,
and by every measure the world uses,
he was untouchable.

Here is what you need
to know before we begin.
He was not caught by a paper trail,

or a clever accountant,
or a jealous rival.

He was caught the way the government
catches mobsters and drug cartels.
They listened. They recorded his phone.

Then, in a courtroom, they
played him back to himself.

So the question of this film
is not whether the rich cheat.
You already suspect that they do.

The real question is harder,
and it is more interesting.

What does it actually
take to catch one of them?

And what did the people
chasing him have to become,
to finally make it stick?

Now hold one more image
next to the billionaire.

On the other side of his trades
sits someone completely ordinary.
A retired teacher.

A nurse moving her
savings into the market.

A young couple buying their first
shares of a company they believe in.

They are playing what
they think is a fair game,

and they have no idea
that the game is not fair.

That is the real injury
at the center of this story.
Not a vault broken open in the night,
but a market tilted in broad daylight,

one secret at a time, against every single
person who actually followed the rules.

To understand why this case
shook the entire industry,
you have to understand one word.
The word runs the whole street.

Edge. On Wall Street, an edge is the thing
you know that the person on the
other side of the trade does not.
Better research. Faster math.
A sharper read of the crowd.

A legal edge is the engine
of the entire business.

Every fund, every desk, every
analyst is hunting for one,
every single hour the market is open.

Raj Rajaratnam was very,
very good at the legal kind.
He was relentless on the phone.

He built a vast web of contacts across
the technology and finance worlds,

and he worked it
constantly, trading gossip,
favors, and reads on companies.

He turned Galleon into one
of the most watched funds of its era,

and the returns made him rich
and made the people around him rich.

Proximity to him felt
like proximity to money.
To the people who worked for him,

Rajaratnam could seem like
the best-connected man alive.

He ran the fund like a newsroom
that never went to sleep,
pulling in fragments from everywhere,

rewarding whoever brought
him something sharp,

and never quite forgetting
whoever showed up empty-handed.

Inside that world, knowing
things was the entire game.
The earlier you knew, the bigger you were.

Most of what reached him
was ordinary and completely legal,
the daily weather of a busy fund.

This story is only about
the part that was not.
But there is a second kind of edge,

and it does not come from working
harder than anyone else.
It comes from knowing first.

Knowing the earnings
before they are announced.
Knowing the takeover before it is signed.

Knowing the bad news while everyone
else is still being told the company is
fine. That kind of edge is not research.

It is theft: information that belongs
to a company and its shareholders,
not to a trader with the right friends.
And that second edge has one beautiful,

terrible feature. It
almost never leaves a mark.

A normal crime gives you
something to point at.
A body. A broken window.

A missing car. This crime is a single
sentence whispered into a telephone.
A number, traded for a number.
And then a trade that looks, on paper,

exactly like a smart guess by a man
already famous for smart guesses.
So ask yourself the question

the government could
not answer for decades.
How do you prove a whisper?
For most of the history of the market,

the honest answer
was that you mostly couldn't.
Regulators could see the suspicious trade.

They could see that someone
bought heavily,

right before the good news,
and sold right before the bad.

But seeing a pattern is not the same
as proving that a specific human being
knew a specific secret.
A suspicious chart is a hunch,

and you cannot send a person
to prison on a hunch.

A jury needs the moment
the secret actually changed hands,
and that moment was always invisible.
Sit with what that meant for a second,

because it is the quiet
engine of the whole problem.

It meant the people most able to cheat
were also the people hardest to catch.
The bigger and more powerful your network,

the more deniable any
single phone call became.
You could always say it was a guess.
You could always say it was research,

a mosaic of public facts
assembled by a brilliant mind.
The edge protected itself.

The better you were at it,
the safer you were.

So a culture grew up
inside that blind spot.

Not everyone — most
of Wall Street is honest,
and most edges really are earned.

But at the very top, among a small set
of people who all knew one another,
a different habit took hold.
Information became a kind of currency.
You gave a secret, and you got one back.

Favors, with a price measured
not in dollars but in tips,
and the tips were worth millions.

And the currency moved
through ordinary friendship,
which is what made it so hard to see.

A college classmate who now
sat on a corporate board.

A consultant who advised everyone
and therefore heard everything.

An executive, flattered to be asked
his opinion by a famous investor.
None of them, on a normal Tuesday,
looked anything like a criminal.
They looked like a contact list.
That was the genius of the thing.
That was also the rot of it.

Rajaratnam sat in the middle
of a web exactly like that.

The government would later argue that it
ran from inside a giant chip company

in the West, through one of the most
famous consulting firms in the world,

and all the way into the boardroom of one
of the most powerful banks on earth.
Secrets came in along those lines.

Trades went out. And the fund kept
beating the market just often enough,

and just quietly enough, to look like
pure genius instead of something else.

For years, that was as close
to a perfect crime as money can buy.
It was quiet. It was wildly profitable,
and it was deniable at every single step.

It was the kind of thing that everyone
in the business suspected was

happening, and that no prosecutor
on earth could actually touch.
If the story had simply stayed there,

in that comfortable shadow, you would
never have heard this man's name.

This matters to you even if you have
never bought a single share in your life.
Your pension owns stocks.
Your retirement account owns stocks.

The savings of almost everyone you
know are quietly riding on one promise.
That the market is roughly fair.

That nobody at the table
can simply see the cards.
When a handful of insiders can see them,
the market stops being a market.

It becomes a private club
with a public entrance,

and the rest of us
are standing in that entrance,

paying full price for a seat
in a game that was already decided.
But somewhere inside the government,

a small group of investigators
got tired of it.
Tired of watching the pattern light up,

again and again, and never being
able to reach the people behind it.
They had the trades.
They had the timing.
They had the suspicion.

What they did not have was the one thing
a jury believes more than any chart,

more than any expert,
more than any theory.
They did not have the words.
So they decided to go and get them.

And to do it, they
reached for a tool that,

until that moment, no one in the country
had ever really aimed at a man in a
good suit.
To see how the secrets actually traveled,
follow four people.
None of them ran a hedge fund.

Each of them simply sat somewhere a fund
manager can only dream of sitting:
inside the company, before the news.

Each was charged separately,
in their own case,
with their own story and their own fate.
But the lines they sat on all ran,
eventually, toward the same telephone.

The first sat inside Intel, one
of the largest chipmakers on earth.

A man named Rajiv Goel, a friend
of Rajaratnam's going back years.

From a seat like that, you can see
a quarter before the public can.

You can know whether the numbers are going
to be good or bad while the rest of

the market is still
guessing, still hoping,
still trading in the dark.

The second sat at McKinsey, the consulting
firm that quietly advises the
giants of the corporate world.
A partner named Anil Kumar.
The government said he was paid,
on the side, for a private stream

of the things he learned
while advising his

clients. The entire promise of a firm
like that is discretion — that your
secrets are safe in the room.
That promise, prosecutors said,
was quietly for sale.
The third sat high inside IBM.
Robert Moffat, a senior executive,

the kind of name that gets floated
as a future chief of the whole company.
And the fourth, Danielle Chiesi,
worked at a fund called New Castle,

and traded in the same
kind of secrets — talking,

the government said, in the careful
half-code of people who know,

somewhere inside, that they should
not be saying this out loud.
Look at that group for one second.
An Intel insider. A McKinsey partner.
An IBM executive. A fund manager.
This was not some back alley.
This was the boardroom, the corner office,
and the consulting suite.

The respectable rooms, the ones
with the good art and the city views.

And inside those rooms,
the government would argue,

the market that millions of ordinary
people trusted with their savings was
being quietly, methodically robbed.

Look again at exactly
where these people sat.
A great chip company.
A legendary consulting firm.
A pillar of American business.
Institutions that run entirely on trust,

on the simple belief that what happens
inside their walls stays inside their

walls. The government's case was that each
of these places had been quietly
hollowed out a little from the inside,

by someone they had trusted
with their most guarded secrets.

The robbery here was not
only of the market.
It was of the institutions themselves,

betrayed by the very people
they had lifted to the top.

Here is how a single
secret turned into money.

An insider learns that a company
is about to be bought.
He picks up the phone.

Minutes later, a fund
is buying that stock — quietly,

in pieces, spread out so that nothing
looks strange to anyone watching.

Days later, the deal
is announced to the public.
The price jumps. The position

that was bought on a whisper
is suddenly worth
millions more than it cost.

Clean. Invisible. Worst
of all, repeatable.

The quiet genius of a network like
this is that nobody inside it ever has to
feel like a criminal.
The insider is only helping a friend.
The friend is only listening.
The favor comes wrapped in dinners,

in shared vacations,
in years of real trust,

until the precise moment a secret
crosses the line is almost impossible to
find. There is no mask.
There is no getaway car.
There is no single dramatic betrayal.
There is just a relationship, slowly bent,
one ordinary conversation at a time,

until the bending quietly becomes
the whole point of the friendship.

Here is the part that should
genuinely unsettle you.
The people feeding those secrets were not,
for the most part, desperate.
They were not stealing to survive.

They were already
successful, already wealthy,

already admired. The temptation
at the top of the world is not survival.

It is certainty. It is the chance to take
the one thing the market is never,
ever supposed to sell, a sure thing,
and to feel, just for a moment,
like a person who simply cannot lose.
What did all of this actually earn?

The honest answer is that it depends
entirely on how you count it.

Different agencies used different
methods and arrived at different numbers,
and we will come back to that gap later,

because the gap itself turns
out to be part of the story.

But by any reasonable count, the trades
that ran on these whispers were worth
tens of millions of dollars.

Now remember the problem
from the first movement.
Every one of these calls sounded,
to anyone listening from the outside,
like two friends simply talking.
Markets. The weather.
Family. A name dropped here.
A number mentioned there.

Nothing a regulator could ever carry
into a courtroom and hand to a jury.
The crime lived entirely in the timing,

and the timing was perfectly,
infuriatingly deniable.

The man at the center of it
understood that completely.

It is a large part of why people
at his level felt so safe.

They were not hiding in some
dark and obvious place.
They were hiding in plain sight,

inside conversations that looked
and sounded completely ordinary,

protected by one simple
and seemingly permanent fact.
No one could hear them.
No one could hear them.

That sentence is the hinge
of the entire story,

so hold onto it. The crime was perfect
for exactly as long as it stayed

unheard. Which meant there was really
only one way left to break it.

Someone was going to have
to start listening.

The investigators who finally moved
on Galleon came at it the slow way,

the patient way. They started
where these cases usually start.

With someone on the inside who agreed
to cooperate — a person who could tell

them where to look, and confirm what
the trades had only ever hinted at.
But a cooperator can always be doubted.

A good defense lawyer can stand
in front of a jury and say,

this person is a liar, this person
is only talking to save their own skin,
do not believe a word of it.

The investigators wanted something
a defense lawyer could not talk their way

around. They wanted evidence that could
not be cross-examined into doubt.
They wanted the calls themselves.

So they did something
that, in a financial case,
was almost unheard of.

They went to a federal judge,
laid out what they had,
and asked for a wiretap.

Court permission to secretly record
a private citizen's telephone.

For decades, that specific power
had been pointed at organized crime,

at drug networks, at the kind of violence
that leaves actual bodies in the
street. It had not been pointed

at a billionaire sitting
behind a Bloomberg
terminal.

Understand how large
a line that was to cross.

A wiretap is the most invasive
tool the government has.
It does not capture one careful,
chosen moment. It captures everything.
Every deal. Every secret.
Every private, foolish, ordinary,

human thing a person says into
a phone across the span of months.
To aim that tool at Wall Street

was to declare something
new and stunning out

loud. The suits would now
be treated exactly like the mob.
The judge said yes.
And in 2008, on Raj Rajaratnam's phone,
the recorders began to turn.

For months, federal agents sat in a quiet
room and listened to a billionaire's
life unfold one call at a time.
Most of it was nothing.
Lunch plans. Complaints.
The grind of an ordinary rich man's day.

They waited, patiently, for the ordinary
chatter to harden into something a
jury would understand.

Consider the people
in that listening room for a moment.
Night after night, headphones
on, transcribing a stranger's entire life.
The dinner plans. The arguments.
The long stretches of pure boredom.
Most of it meant absolutely nothing,

and sitting through all
of that nothing was the actual job.
They were waiting for a single sentence.

The one moment when a careful man
finally forgot to be careful and said out

loud the thing the trades
had only ever whispered.

Patience, it turned out, was the one
weapon the men at the top had never
planned for.
Eventually, it did.

Because here is the strange
truth about feeling untouchable.

The longer it lasts,
the less careful you become.

On a tapped line,
the government would later say,

the scheme stopped being an abstract
pattern of trades and became a plain

conversation. People discussed information
they were never supposed to have.

They discussed it directly,
in their own voices,
with their own names attached,

into a phone they were absolutely
certain was private.

That is the moment the whole
world quietly tilts.

For the entire history
of this kind of crime,
the secret had been invisible,

untouchable, impossible
to hold in your hand.
Now it was on tape.
The whisper had a waveform.

The deniable phone call had
become a recording — time-stamped,
in the speaker's own unmistakable voice,

sitting in a government
evidence locker, waiting.

And you cannot tell a jury
that a recording is only guessing.
You cannot say the tape was confused,

or jealous, or just assembling
a clever mosaic of public facts.

The defense that had protected the very
top of Wall Street for generations,

the comfortable line
that it was only talk,

only research, simply does not
survive the sound of your own voice,
calmly saying otherwise.

There is something
uncomfortable in all of this,

and the honest version
of the story has to admit it.

A government that can
listen to a billionaire can,
in principle, listen to anyone.

The very same tool that finally caught
the guilty could just as easily be
turned to frighten the innocent.
The question waiting at the end

of this case was never
only whether one man

had done it. It was whether a free
country should hand itself a power this

large, and then trust that it would
only ever be pointed at the people who
truly deserved it.
On the morning of October sixteenth,

2009, it ended the way these
things end in the movies,
except that it was completely real.
Agents came to the door.

They arrested Raj Rajaratnam at his home
and walked him out — a billionaire in
handcuffs, in front of the cameras,
on the morning news.

That same day, federal prosecutors
and the SEC stepped up to the microphones
and announced the charges.

The image went around
the world that morning.

A man who had spent his whole life
as the person everyone else called for

answers was now the person
being walked to a car.

For everyone who had ever quietly
suspected the game was rigged,

and assumed nothing would ever
actually be done about it,

that single picture said something
simple and almost unbelievable.

Sometimes, the people at the very
top do get the knock on the door.

Within days, the seven-billion-dollar
fund began to close down.
The contacts stopped returning calls.

The empire that had taken years to build
came apart in a matter of weeks.

Because the one thing that had truly
held it all together had never been the
trades. It had been the silence,
and that silence was over.
But an arrest is not a conviction,
and Raj Rajaratnam did not fold.

He hired one of the finest
defense teams that money can buy,

and then he made a choice that most
people in his position never make.
He refused to plead guilty.

He decided to take
the whole thing to a jury,

and he bet — everything —
that the tapes would not be enough.
The trial opened in Manhattan in 2011,

and more than anything
else, it turned on sound.

The prosecutors did not simply stand
up and describe the scheme in their own
words. They played it.

They sat the jury down, and they let
twelve ordinary people listen to the
defendant's own recorded phone calls.
Again, and again. Until the abstract,

bloodless idea of insider trading
became something else entirely — a human
voice, filling a silent courtroom.

The defense did everything
it possibly could.

It argued the trades
were built on research,

on public information, on the ordinary
mosaic of facts that any sharp analyst
assembles every day.
For years, in case after case,
that argument had worked.

It had been the great escape
hatch at the top of the market.

But it is very, very hard
to talk over a recording.

The jury did not have
to imagine the crime.
They could hear it.

The defense even had
a name for its argument.
The mosaic theory.

The idea that a brilliant analyst builds
a picture out of a thousand small,
public, perfectly legal pieces,
the way a mosaic is built from tiles,

and that what looks from the outside
like a stolen secret is really just an
unusually good guess.

For years, that picture had
been almost impossible to take apart.

It was the perfect defense
for an invisible crime.
The trouble, this time, was simple.
The tapes did not show a mosaic.
They showed a phone call.
On May eleventh, 2011, the jury came back.
Guilty. And not on a few of the counts,
as a kind of split decision.

On all fourteen. Five
counts of conspiracy.
Nine counts of securities fraud.

The man that everyone in the business
had called untouchable had just been

convicted, in open court, by twelve
completely ordinary people who had spent
weeks doing nothing but listening to him.
When the foreman said the word guilty,

fourteen times over, something cracked
in that room that was far bigger than
one man. For a whole generation,

the people at the very top had
operated on a kind of unspoken promise.
That the rules quietly bent for them.

That the worst thing that could
ever really happen was a fine,

a settlement, an uncomfortable
week in the newspapers.

A billionaire in a federal prison
cell was never part of that deal.
The verdict tore the promise up,

in public, where everyone in every
corner office could see it.
Five months later, on October thirteenth,
2011, the sentence came down.
Eleven years in federal prison.

At the time, prosecutors called it
the longest prison sentence ever handed
down in an American insider-trading case.

The number was not just
a punishment for one man.

It was a message, fired down
the entire length of Wall Street,

meant to be heard in every
corner office in the country.
Then came the money.

The court ordered him to forfeit more
than fifty-three million dollars,

and to pay a ten-million-dollar
fine on top of it.

And in a separate civil case, the SEC
won a record penalty of more than

ninety-two million dollars, the largest
it had ever obtained against a single
individual in an insider-trading case.

Add it all together, and the penalties
against him passed a hundred and
fifty-six million dollars.

Now, finally, come back
to that gap in the profit numbers.
Depending on who was counting,

and how, the illegal gains were put
at anywhere from twenty-odd million
dollars to over sixty.
We do not actually need one clean,

final figure, and you should
be suspicious of anyone who hands you one.

The court's own number, the more than
fifty million dollars he was forced to

give back, already says
everything it needs to say.
The case did not stop with one man.

Regulators eventually brought civil
charges against twenty-nine people and

firms across the wider
Galleon investigation,

and the broader sweep ended in dozens
of convictions and guilty pleas.
The whisper network, it turned out,
had a great many nodes.

This was never the story
of a single bad apple.
It was the story of an orchard.

And one of those lines reached
as high as the case would ever go.
In a completely separate trial,

with its own jury, a former Goldman
Sachs board member named Rajat Gupta was

convicted in 2012 of feeding Rajaratnam
secrets from inside one of the most
powerful banks in the world.
He was sentenced to two years.

His was a different case,
a different verdict,

a different punishment,
but it answered the oldest,
most cynical question about Wall Street.

Did the rot reach all the way
to the very top? Yes. It did.
Rajaratnam's lawyers appealed,

and they aimed straight
at the heart of the case.

The wiretaps. If the recordings
could be thrown out,

then everything built upon
them might collapse with them.
This was the real test.

Not whether he had done it — the jury
had answered that — but whether the

government had ever been allowed
to listen in the first place.

In 2013, the appeals
court gave its answer.

It upheld the wiretaps
as lawfully authorized.
It ruled that the recordings could stand,
and it affirmed the conviction.
The method was now blessed by the courts.

Listening to Wall Street the same
way you listen to the mob was,
the judges said, entirely legal.

A door that had been shut
for a century had been opened,
and it was not going to close again.
Raj Rajaratnam served most of his term.

In 2019, he was released
to home confinement.
He has never accepted the verdict.

In a memoir, he still insists that he
was wronged — a research-driven trader,

he says, caught in a net
that was cast far too wide.
You are allowed to hear that.
To be fair, you should.
But the appeals court heard it too,

and it disagreed, and the conviction
stands today exactly as the jury
delivered it.
So go back to the question we opened with.
Not whether the rich cheat.
You never doubted that.

The question was what it
actually takes to catch one.
Now you have the answer.

It took the government deciding
to treat a billionaire like a gangster.

It took a judge's signature
granting permission to listen.

And in the end, it took the one piece
of evidence that even the most powerful

man in the room cannot
argue with: himself.
That is why this case still matters,
all these years later.

Not because one more fund
manager went to prison.

But because of the day the most protected
people in the country learned that
the line had quietly moved.

That the old defense, the easy
claim that it was only talk,
could now be recorded, and frozen,

and played back in their own calm voice
to twelve strangers in a jury box.
The whisper was no longer safe,
and everyone at the top knew it.

Most stories about Wall
Street end with a shrug,

because most of them end
with no one really paying.
A fine that costs less than the crime.

A settlement with no
admission of anything.

A famous name that is quietly
back in business by spring.
This one ends differently, and

that difference
is the entire reason to tell
it. A man at the very top was caught,
convicted, and sent to prison,

on the strength of nothing more
than his own recorded voice.

The system is not really built to do
that to its most powerful people.
Once, against the odds, it did.

The system does not catch the people
at the very top very often.

This is the story of one
of the times that it did.

If that matters to you — if you want
more stories about how the powerful are
finally held to account, told straight,

and told carefully, then
subscribe to the channel,
and hit the like button below,
so that the next one finds its way to you.

Stay curious, and we will
see you in the next one.
